issues.legal_issue: A clear and comprehensive statutory scheme is not confined by a narrower description of its purpose in the statement of objects and reasons.
material_facts: The statute allowed an agriculturist debtor to seek restoration of property sold in execution, including sales completed before the statute came into force.
The challengers argued that the statement of objects and reasons focused on debts incurred after an earlier relief law and therefore did not support setting aside earlier completed sales.
The statute's provisions were clear, and the statement of objects and reasons also described the proposed legislation as comprehensive.
issues.conclusion: The statutory scheme was not limited by the statement of objects and reasons, and the provision for setting aside qualifying sales was not beyond the statute's stated purpose.
issues.legal_principle: Where statutory provisions are clear and unambiguous, their scope need not be restricted by the statement of objects and reasons. The Court relied on the comprehensive character of the legislation and the clear provisions governing the relief.

predicates.statutory_text_is_clear: The enacted provisions clearly state the circumstances in which a debtor may seek restoration of property sold in execution.
predicates.scheme_is_comprehensive: The legislation addresses relief for indebted agriculturists across more than the particular situation emphasized in its statement of objects and reasons.
predicates.objects_statement_is_relied_on_to_narrow: A challenger relies on the statement of objects and reasons to argue that the enacted provisions have a narrower reach.
predicates.challenge_to_statutory_scope: The proceeding challenges whether a statutory provision reaches the transactions or events at issue.

issues.definition: When the statutory text is clear and the scheme is comprehensive, or a challenger uses the objects statement to narrow that text, the statute's scope is not narrowed by the objects statement.

issues.legal_issue: A state legislature may provide agricultural debt relief for agriculturists whose property was sold to discharge their debts, even when the debt no longer subsists.
material_facts: The law provided relief to agriculturists whose immovable property had been sold in execution to recover a debt.
The challengers argued that the state legislature could not legislate about a debt that had already been discharged by the sale.
The relief addressed agriculturists who had lost property and the means of livelihood through distress sales.
issues.conclusion: The state legislature was competent to enact the debt-relief provision, including relief for agriculturists whose debts had been discharged through sales of their property.
issues.legal_principle: Article 246(3) of the Constitution gives a state legislature exclusive power over matters in List II, and Entry 30 of List II includes money-lending and relief of agricultural indebtedness. That entry is not confined to subsisting debts and encompasses relief for agriculturists who lost property through execution sales. The Court relied on Fatehchand Himmatlal v. State of Maharashtra and the principle of liberal construction of constitutional legislative entries stated in Navinchandra Mafatlal v. Commissioner of Income-tax.

predicates.state_legislation_addresses_agricultural: A state legislature enacts a law providing relief to indebted agriculturists.
predicates.relief_covers_property_lost_to_discharge: The law provides relief to an agriculturist whose property was sold to discharge the debt, even though the debt no longer subsists.
predicates.challenge_to_state_legislative_competenc: The proceeding challenges the state legislature's authority to enact the relief measure.

issues.definition: When state legislation provides agricultural debt relief that covers property lost to discharge a debt, a challenge to the state's legislative competence does not invalidate that legislation.

issues.legal_issue: Restoring property sold in execution to an agriculturist debtor, subject to repayment and compensation for improvements, is a reasonable restriction on the purchaser's right to hold property.
material_facts: The law allowed an agriculturist debtor to seek restoration of qualifying property sold in execution of a debt decree.
A decree-holder purchaser could receive the purchase money in instalments, while a stranger purchaser was entitled to the purchase money in a lump sum.
The debtor had to repay the purchase money, and the value of improvements made by the purchaser had to be deposited for payment to the purchaser.
The law was directed at agricultural indebtedness and the severe poverty of indebted agriculturists.
issues.conclusion: The restriction on the purchasers' property rights was reasonable and did not violate the constitutional guarantee of the right to hold property.
issues.legal_principle: Article 19(1)(f), read with Article 19(5), permits reasonable restrictions on the right to hold property in the interests of the general public. Reasonableness requires balancing the nature of the right and the harm to its holder against the social purpose, urgency of the problem, and connection between the restriction and that purpose; Articles 38 and 39(b) also inform that assessment. The Court relied on Kesavananda Bharati v. State of Kerala, State of Kerala v. N. M. Thomas, Fatehchand Himmatlal v. State of Maharashtra, Jyoti Prashad v. Administrator for the Union Territory of Delhi, Mohd. Hanif Quareshi v. State of Bihar, Chintaman Rao v. State of Madhya Pradesh, State of Madras v. V. G. Row, Narendra Kumar v. Union of India, Bachan Singh v. State of Punjab, Kavalappara Kottarathil Kochuni v. State of Madras, and O. K. Ghosh v. E. X. Joseph.

rule.if: challenge_to_property_right_restriction and relief_targets_poor_indebted_agriculturists and purchaser_receives_repayment and (improvements_are_compensated or purchaser_is_paid_before_restoration)

predicates.challenge_to_property_right_restriction: The proceeding challenges a law that restricts a purchaser's ability to retain property acquired at a sale.
predicates.relief_targets_poor_indebted_agriculturi: The law is directed at relieving poor agriculturists burdened by debt and distress sales.
predicates.purchaser_receives_repayment: The law requires the debtor to repay the purchase money to the purchaser.
predicates.improvements_are_compensated: The law requires the debtor to deposit the value of qualifying improvements for payment to the purchaser.
predicates.purchaser_is_paid_before_restoration: The law makes restoration conditional on payment of the amount due to the purchaser.

issues.definition: When a challenged property restriction targets poor indebted agriculturists and provides repayment to the purchaser, including compensation for improvements or payment before restoration, the restriction is reasonable.

issues.legal_issue: Preferential relief for economically backward agriculturist debtors and different treatment of decree-holder and stranger purchasers are reasonable classifications.
material_facts: The law provided special relief to agriculturist debtors because they were poor and economically backward.

A decree-holder who had purchased the property could receive half the purchase money initially and the balance in instalments, while a stranger purchaser was entitled to the entire purchase money in a lump sum.

Decree-holder purchasers were treated separately because they were creditors who had obtained the decrees and were viewed as more likely to exploit debtors; court rules also restricted their ability to bid without permission.
issues.conclusion: The classification of agriculturist debtors for preferential relief and the different treatment of decree-holder and stranger purchasers did not violate the constitutional guarantee of equality.
issues.legal_principle: Article 14 forbids hostile discrimination but permits reasonable classification founded on an intelligible differentia that has a rational nexus to the statutory object. Persons in materially different positions may be treated differently; decree-holder purchasers could be treated as a distinct class, and economically backward agriculturist debtors could receive preferential relief. The Court relied on Shri Ram Krishna Dalmia v. Shri Justice S. R. Tendolkar, State of Kerala v. N. M. Thomas, State of West Bengal v. Anwar Ali Sarkar, and Order XXI, Rule 72 of the Code of Civil Procedure.

predicates.challenge_to_equality_classification: The proceeding alleges that a law's different treatment of groups violates equality before the law.
predicates.beneficiaries_are_economically_backward_: The group receiving preferential treatment consists of economically backward debtors in need of relief.
predicates.classification_tracks_relevant_differenc: The distinctions between the groups reflect relevant differences, such as a purchaser's role as creditor or stranger to the debt.
predicates.measure_advances_debt_relief: The classifications are connected to the purpose of relieving indebted debtors.

issues.definition: When a challenged classification gives relief to economically backward debtors, tracks relevant differences among the affected groups, and advances debt relief, the classification is valid.

issues.legal_issue: Protecting a bona fide transferee of property from an auction purchaser while allowing restoration claims against the auction purchaser does not discriminate between equals.
material_facts: The law exempted a bona fide transferee who acquired rights from an auction purchaser before publication of the relevant bill.
The appellant was a stranger who purchased the property at a court auction arising from execution of a debt decree.

A court-auction purchaser knew the property was being sold to satisfy a debtor's liability, while a bona fide transferee acquired the property through a negotiated transaction without notice of the debt or the circumstances of the decree.
The law provided for payment of the auction purchaser's purchase money and qualifying improvement costs.
issues.conclusion: A stranger auction purchaser and a bona fide transferee were not similarly situated, so protecting the transferee did not amount to hostile discrimination against the auction purchaser.
issues.legal_principle: Article 14 prohibits discrimination between persons who are similarly situated, not different treatment of persons whose relevant circumstances differ. A court-auction purchaser who knows the sale arises from execution against the debtor is materially different from a bona fide transferee who purchases through negotiation without notice. The Court relied on State of Jammu and Kashmir v. T. N. Khosa, Chiranjit Lal Chowdhuri v. Union of India, Southern Railway Co. v. Greene, and the principle underlying protection of bona fide transferees under section 53 of the Transfer of Property Act and section 27(b) of the Specific Relief Act.

rule.if: challenge_to_equality_classification and purchaser_acquired_at_distress_sale and transferee_acquired_without_notice_through_negotiation and purchaser_receives_repayment

predicates.challenge_to_equality_classification: The proceeding alleges that different treatment of affected property holders violates equality before the law.
predicates.purchaser_acquired_at_distress_sale: The purchaser acquired the property at a court sale to satisfy a debt against the debtor.
predicates.transferee_acquired_without_notice_throu: A later transferee acquired the property through a negotiated transaction without notice of the debt or the circumstances of the execution sale.
predicates.purchaser_receives_repayment: The law provides for repayment of the auction purchaser's purchase money.

issues.definition: When an auction purchaser acquired property at a distress sale, a transferee acquired it through negotiation without notice, and the purchaser receives repayment, their different treatment is not hostile discrimination.
